{
 "summary": "Pass Bitcoin Core's compiler and linker hardening flags to the embedded libsecp256k1 build. The change factors hardening flags into a dedicated CMake interface library (`hardening_interface`) linked by `core_interface` and forwards those options to the secp256k1 subtree configuration.",
 "problem": "The secp256k1 subtree does not inherit flags from `core_interface`, leaving its compiled objects without hardening flags such as stack protection, stack clash protection, and control-flow integrity flags. Because linkers omit binary-wide control-flow protection markers (like AArch64 BTI/PAC or x86_64 CET) if even a single linked object lacks them, the missing flags strip control-flow protections from the final executable on toolchains that do not enable them by default.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'On aarch64 Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15 this also costs the whole binary its control flow property: master's bitcoind has no AArch64 feature note, and the three secp256k1 objects are the only ones in the build tree without it.'",
  "PR description: 'With it, the same build shows AArch64 feature: BTI, PAC, GCS on bitcoind.'"
 ],

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.
